chunks: From him, from Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā al-ʿUbaydī, from Durust, from Ibrāhīm ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd, from Abī al-Ḥasan عليه السلام, who said:

The Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله entered upon ʿĀʾishah while she had placed her water vessel in the sun. He said: “O Ḥumayrāʾ, what is this?” She said: “I am washing my head and body.” He said: “Do not do it again, for it causes leprosy.”

Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan said: This report is to be understood as indicating a kind of dislikedness, not prohibition, because there is no harm in using water that has been left in the sun. And that which clarifies what we have mentioned [follows].

key_terms.أَغْسِلُ: I wash; used here for washing the head and body
key_terms.الْبَرَصَ: leprosy; mentioned here as an effect attributed in the report
key_terms.الْكَرَاهِيَةِ: dislikedness in legal usage, short of prohibition
key_terms.الْمِيَاهِ: waters; referring here to water left in the sun
key_terms.بِاسْتِعْمَالِهِ: by using it; meaning its practical use

ai.seo_question: Is using water left in the sun for ghusl forbidden or merely disliked in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This report discusses using water that has been heated or left in the sun for washing the body. Al-Ṭūsī explains that the wording indicates karāhah (dislikedness), not prohibition, and that using such water is not unlawful. The narration is therefore treated within fiqh as guidance on ritual purity and usage of water, not as an absolute ban.
